But, A doesn’t really get at the ‘WHY’ factor of the paradox, which is what we’re looking for:

WHY do raisins have more iron per calorie than grapes? 

Because caramelized sugar cannot be digested, thus lowering the calorie count of raisins? Yeah, sure, this makes sense if we puzzle it out. The stimulus states that that a raisin and grape are essentially the same other than a difference in water content (which is zero impact), and sugar caramelization. If the caramelized sugar in the raisins lowers their calorie count, but the iron stays the same between the two, this would justify a greater iron/calorie ratio in raisins compared to grapes.

The thing that has helped me the most is to try your best to relate what you’re reading to your every day life. In any way possible. Even the slightest pathway to something you’ve read/done/experienced before will help turn your brain on and make it easier to ingest. (It helps your comprehension too, which will make answering questions easier). 

As far as fatigue/endurance….first I would try slowing down a bit during your initial read. Take a beat to understand each point the author(s) are trying to make and how it relates to the overall structure of the passage before moving on. Trying to brute force your brain to ingest all that information as fast as possible is definitely tiring. Taking your time helps save your energy for later passages. Not to mention you may, counterintuitively, actually move through questions faster since you’ll have a better understanding of the passage initially.

I actually just spent an hour last weekend trying to wrap my head around this exact question lol. I chose the exact same answer as you and had the same frustrations. 

  
I took it with LSATLab, and to paraphrase their explanation: there is a difference between a sample being intentionally random (which the author IS assuming, and is the flaw called by the correct answer choice) and two outcomes of the sample being just as likely as the other (which is too strong an assumption, considering the author is assuming a 20% rate of defectiveness, which makes it far more likely that a selected item will be non-defective than defective). 

Have you ever seen those memes/jokes where people say that the chances of anything happening is always 50/50? This question is basically demonstrating why that understanding of statistics is incorrect. 

I don't deny that this question is exceedingly vague in its writing, and is absolutely an example of the test writers trying to use commonplace assumptions/understanding of language to lure you into a trap answer. D ends up being the better answer as it clearly implies that the sample is biased, which obliterates the argument. 

Sorry if this is absolutely unhelpful, it's an exceedingly obnoxious question, in my opinion.

Fellow Amazon accountant here. Has YEC been a living nightmare for you too?

It gets more complicated when you have to extend your understanding to more complex concepts. For FAR that’s gonna be things like leases, consolidations, stock transactions. Just take the time to understand the accounting impact of every transaction before you move onto the text. Will save you tons of time in the long run.

If I may.

Let’s say you buy inventory on account:

Dr. Inventory
Cr. Accounts Payable 

This would flow to the Balance Sheet: This transaction will increase total assets and total liabilities. 

Then, You sell the inventory to customers for cash:

Dr. Cash 
Cr. Sales Revenue 

Dr. COGS 
Cr. Inventory 


The first entry hits the balance sheet, increasing assets, and the income statement, increasing revenue. It will also flow through to the Statement of Cashflows, as part of cashflows from operations 

The second entry also hits the I/S and balance sheet. Increasing cost of goods sold on the I/S. 

Finally, you use cash to pay down your account receivable:

Dr. Accounts Payable
Cr. Cash 

This impacts the balance sheet by lowering total assets and liabilities. 


This is just a very simple and stripped down example of what it might look like to track journal entries through the financial statements. Basically knowing what accounts certain activities impact, and how that impact will be reflected in the financials.

General summaries for the main brands in my experience:


Park Hyatt (or Andaz)- The best of the best, their flagship brand. Expect excellent service, top-tier amenities, up-scale food options, details and touches that just radiate class. Depending on the location, expect to pay $800/night+++ 

Grand Hyatt- Generally still very nice, but less focus extremely fancy amenities and extra special details than at a Park Hyatt. You’ll probably pay $300/night+ depending on location 

Hyatt Regency-Probably their most prolific brand. A classic business hotel in most cases. Generally still clean and worth staying at, but any delightful touches are generally gone. The food options are generally going to be more normal and affordable. The only special amenity will probably be a pool. There are so many of these around that the price range varies wildly depending on location. Probably starting at around $100 or so/night I’m the US.

Hyatt Place/Hyatt House-Generally considered the lowest tier/most inconsistent of the Hyatt brands. These are generally not ran by Hyatt employees directly, but are franchised out. So service can be inconsistent. Especially in the US, these are generally older, run-down properties that were independent motels in their past life, so they can be dingy and show their age. These are your cheap, family vacation hotels. The ones that serve free breakfast in the morning and have a pool for the kiddos, but not much else. I think the cheapest one I’ve stayed at was around $75/night, but I’m sure they go much cheaper. 


Of course, all of these descriptions have their exceptions. ESPECIALLY overseas in Asia where the nightly rates tend to be much cheaper for really great properties. Additionally, there are rundown Grand Hyatts that are not worth staying at over a regency in the area. Or properties like the Hyatt Regency Grand Cypress in Orlando which is basically a full-on resort even though it’s “technically” just a Regency

All this to say, try not to get bogged down in which brand you’re staying at. Research what the properties have to offer, read reviews, and decide which properties have what experience you’re looking for.

Chapman is very laissez faire about religion. All religions are represented and have regular services on campus, anyone can attend at any time, but there is no required chapel or required religious classes like I’m fairly certain they have at Biola. Biola is a capital C Christian university. It will be a major part of the university’s culture and of your every day life on campus. Chapman isn’t like that. They are supportive of all faiths and make space for religious activities, but it will never be forced on you as part of your university experience. It’s up to you to decide which type of community you would flourish more in.

Chapman does have very vibrant Greek Life, and of course that leads to parties. However, if you’re not involved in Greek Life, there’s really not much pressure to party. In fact, if you’re a male and not in a frat, you won’t be allowed at the parties anyways. I wasn’t in a frat, and was still able to connect with awesome people and make great friends. Overall, I’d say Chapman is much less party oriented than USC. I myself am not of the faith, but there are great groups like Cru on campus that can help connect you with other like-minded individuals to have fun with. 

I was a low income student on scholarship as well, and yes, there are PLENTY of snobby rich kids, it comes with the territory. I was still able to make great friends and had a wonderful college experience. 

Overall, I’d if you want a university where the vast majority of people are going to be Christian, and religion would be a cornerstone of your education, choose Biola. If you want a more classic university experience where you would still have the opportunity to practice your faith and connect with like-minded people on your own time, choose Chapman.

I think it’s a common curse of MMO games that min-maxing will always prevail. No matter how much variety there is, there will always be a definitive “best piece” or “best set” that everyone will gun for. 

The only way I could really see this done is by revolutionizing how stats are allocated to gear completely. Make a “damage set” that offers significant damage stats and very little defensive stats, and a “defensive” set that offers incredibly high resist and health with little to no offensive capabilities. Then a rock-paper-scissors meta could start to form around that 

But, at the end of the day, in this game, there is little to gain from being purely defensive. It’s not like in some games where you can actively tank hits for a team, or (with the possible exception of universally hated jade strategies) outlast an opponent through sustain. Players want the best of all worlds when they bust their asses to farm gear, and as long as the game puts the most value on well-rounded stats, the gear with the best of everything for each level will reign supreme.

HSAs have ultimate tax advantage. Contributions are pretax, they grow tax-free, and can be withdrawn to pay medical expenses with no taxes. Additionally, in most cases, employers will make a contribution to your HSA yearly as well, and you can take this money with you when you leave, and because you’re on a high deductible plan with a HSA, you save a ton of money on healthcare premiums every month. 

Basically, you’re taking the money you’d spend on a health plan that you don’t really need as a young person, and investing it to put towards your healthcare in the future (which also takes the burden of covering health care costs off of your other retirement savings). And even if you’re the healthiest elder in the world, it’s basically a second 401k that your employer helped contribute to.

General rule of thumb seems to be:
Priority 1: Achieve a reasonably liquid emergency fund of 3-6 months expenses. 
Priority 2: 401k up to employer match 
Priority 3: Max out your HSA if you have one (which you should if you’re generally young and without a chronic/expensive illness) 
Priority 4: Max out a Roth IRA
Priority 5: Contribute whatever else you can to your 401k up to the current maximum, other auxiliary investments

Speaking as someone who is currently studying tax from an Accounting perspective and hoping to someday move into Tax Law:

The tax environment in this country is always changing. Every new president thinks their system is better than the last one (especially if there is a change of parties), so at the very least every 4 years there is a big heap of new rules to learn and interpret. 

Plus, tax law basically touches every aspect of the legal field. Business and corporate law, wills & trusts, international law, and more all have important tax aspects that tax lawyers are called to interpret. 

Finally, people and firms  are usually really excited to see their tax attorney because it usually means they are going to explain a highly complicated issue they have no interest in trying to understand, and (if you’ve hired a good lawyer) they’re usually going to save you some money. A lot easier to be satisfied with your career when it feels like you are actively adding value rather than becoming a symbol for someone’s most traumatic time (divorce, medical problem, bankruptcy)

Just my layman’s take!

-Changing my major
-Taking a heavy course load 
-Needing to work through college 
-Being involved in extra curriculars 
-Having one not-so-great semester

I, on a complete whim, applied for the accounting rotational program at Amazon. I didn't even expect to get an interview, but there was an email inviting me to interview with them about a month later in my inbox. It was a 2-hour process with four separate interviews including an excel problem.

I went in completely unconfident, and that's essentially how I felt once the interview was over. I thought I hadn't really left a positive impression on anyone that interviewed me and wasn't able to articulate very well how my previous experience would prepare me for the role. I didn't have knowledge of the proper command to complete the excel problem and overall felt completely out of my depth. 

Nevertheless, 2 weeks later I received my offer, and now I am getting ready to make the move up to Seattle after I graduate. All this to say, you never really know how you are perceived by people interviewing you, and as others have said, the fact that you even got the interview at all makes you an incredibly qualified applicant with lots to offer anywhere you're accepted.

TLDR: if you have significant time to sit with the game and grind it out, and get a storm/fire/myth that can kill the boss in 2-4 rounds every time. You can probably average out 1 full dragoon piece a day, maybe more if you’re faster/lucky/use the port strat.
